replies.text:
I'll analyze EVAL-06 for security threats using STRIDE methodology, focusing on the shared secret JWT authentication design.

**Key Security Concerns:**
- Shared HS256 secret across all services creates single point of failure
- 7-day token validity with no revocation mechanism
- Environment variable storage exposes secrets
- No service-level authorization or identity attribution

Here's the complete threat model:

```json
{
  "schema": "redline.threatmodel.v1",
  "issueKey": "EVAL-06",
  "sketch": {
    "components": ["JWT token", "Shared HS256 secret", "Environment variables", "Microservices", "Service-to-service API calls"],
    "dataStores": [],
    "externalServices": [],
    "trustBoundaries": ["Between microservices"],
    "dataClasses": ["credentials"],
    "exposure": "internal",
    "llmFeatures": false
  },
  "threats": [
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "Shared secret allows any compromised service to impersonate all others",
      "scenario": "An attacker compromises one microservice through vulnerability or insider access, extracts the shared HS256 secret from environment variables, and forges JWTs to impersonate any service. With this single secret, they make unauthorized API calls, access sensitive data, or perform privileged operations as any trusted service. The blast radius of one compromise is the entire service mesh.",
      "component": "Shared HS256 secret",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "JWTs signed using a shared HS256 secret that is stored in each service's environment variables" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V2.8.5", "V2.8.6"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-287", "CWE-798"],
      "plainLanguage": "If one service gets hacked, the attacker can pretend to be any other service because they all use the same password",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Use asymmetric keys for service authentication",
        "given": "microservices need to authenticate each other",
        "when": "a service receives a request from another service",
        "then": "it must verify the caller's identity using public key cryptography where each service has its own private key"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "ElevationOfPrivilege",
      "title": "No service-level authorization with shared secret",
      "scenario": "Using a shared secret means any service can call any other service's endpoints. An attacker who compromises a low-privilege service like logging can use the shared secret to call high-privilege services like payment processing or user management. There's no way to enforce least-privilege because all services share the same credential.",
      "component": "JWT token",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "JWTs signed using a shared HS256 secret" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V4.1.3", "V4.1.5"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-269"],
      "plainLanguage": "Every service can call every other service with the same secret, so compromising the least important service gives access to the most critical ones",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Implement service-level authorization",
        "given": "each microservice has different privilege requirements",
        "when": "a service receives an authenticated request",
        "then": "it must verify the calling service is authorized for that specific operation using unique service identities"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Shared secret exposed in environment variables across all services",
      "scenario": "The shared HS256 secret appears in environment variables of every microservice. An attacker extracts it through process listings, debug endpoints that dump environment, error messages with environment context, container dashboards, CI/CD logs, or memory dumps. Once extracted from any service, it compromises all services.",
      "component": "Environment variables",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "shared HS256 secret that is stored in each service's environment variables" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V2.10.4"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-526", "CWE-215"],
      "plainLanguage": "The secret password in environment variables can leak through error messages, logs, or admin panels, and one leak compromises everything",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Use secure secret storage",
        "given": "services need cryptographic secrets",
        "when": "a service starts or needs to authenticate",
        "then": "it must retrieve secrets from a dedicated secret management system like Vault or AWS Secrets Manager with access controls and audit logging"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "Long-lived tokens remain valid after compromise",
      "scenario": "JWTs valid for 7 days mean stolen tokens from logs, network traffic, or memory dumps let attackers impersonate services for up to a week. Even if the compromise is detected and the service patched, the stolen token continues working. The only mitigation is rotating the shared secret, requiring coordinated redeployment of all services.",
      "component": "JWT token",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Tokens are valid for 7 days" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V2.8.3"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-613"],
      "plainLanguage": "Stolen authentication tokens work for 7 days even after you discover the theft, with no way to cancel them",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Implement short-lived tokens with refresh",
        "given": "JWTs are used for service authentication",
        "when": "a token is issued",
        "then": "it must expire within 1 hour and services must use a refresh mechanism with rotation detection"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Repudiation",
      "title": "Cannot attribute actions to specific services after compromise",
      "scenario": "With a shared secret, all services appear identical in JWT signatures. If the secret is compromised and an attacker forges tokens, there's no way to determine which service was actually compromised, which calls were legitimate versus forged, or which services need incident response. Audit logs show valid JWTs but can't distinguish legitimate services from an attacker with the shared secret.",
      "component": "Shared HS256 secret",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "JWTs signed using a shared HS256 secret" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V2.8.6"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-778"],
      "plainLanguage": "If someone steals the shared password, you can't tell which service was hacked or which API calls were real versus fake",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Ensure unique service identity in tokens",
        "given": "audit logs record service-to-service calls",
        "when": "investigating a security incident",
        "then": "each JWT must contain a unique service identifier backed by individual credentials that allow attribution of all actions"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "JWT algorithm confusion attack possible",
      "scenario": "If JWT libraries allow algorithm switching based on the token's header, an attacker exploits algorithm confusion by creating a JWT with alg none or switching from HS256 to RS256, treating the shared HMAC secret as an RSA public key. Because the secret is widely distributed, an attacker who obtains it crafts tokens that bypass signature verification in vulnerable JWT implementations.",
      "component": "JWT token",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "JWTs signed using a shared HS256 secret" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V2.8.7"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-347"],
      "plainLanguage": "An attacker might trick the system into accepting tokens with no signature or the wrong signature type by changing the algorithm field",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Enforce strict JWT algorithm validation",
        "given": "JWTs are verified",
        "when": "a service receives a JWT",
        "then": "it must reject tokens unless the algorithm in the header exactly matches the expected algorithm configured in code, not from the token"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "DenialOfService",
      "title": "Secret rotation requires coordinated downtime",
      "scenario": "When the shared secret needs rotation after compromise, security audit, or policy, every service must update simultaneously. During rotation either all services restart at once causing downtime, or there's a window with mixed secrets causing authentication failures. Emergency rotation after a breach requires accepting downtime or continued risk. Operational complexity discourages regular rotation, extending exposure.",
      "component": "Shared HS256 secret",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "shared HS256 secret that is stored in each service's environment variables" }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-320"],
      "plainLanguage": "Changing the shared password requires updating and restarting all services at once, causing downtime or authentication failures",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Support graceful secret rotation",
        "given": "secrets need periodic rotation",
        "when": "rotating authentication credentials",
        "then": "services must support dual-secret validation accepting both old and new with automated rollover to avoid downtime"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Tampering",
      "title": "No protection against replay attacks",
      "scenario": "JWTs have no unique identifiers or timestamps that services track. An attacker who intercepts a valid JWT replays it multiple times within the 7-day window. They could replay a token to repeatedly call privilege checks or non-idempotent operations like initiating expensive operations, causing resource exhaustion or business logic abuse.",
      "component": "JWT token",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Tokens are valid for 7 days" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V2.8.3"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-294"],
      "plainLanguage": "An attacker who copies a valid token can use it repeatedly for 7 days with no way to detect or stop duplicate requests",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Implement replay attack protection",
        "given": "service calls should not be replayable",
        "when": "a service receives a JWT",
        "then": "it must validate a unique token identifier and timestamps, and optionally track recently used tokens to prevent replay"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```
